documents.abstract: The study examined occupational hazards common among pig farmers and workers in the Southern Senatorial District of Cross River State, Nigeria. The research was guided with four research purposes and questions, and three hypotheses. Survey design was adopted and farm owners, workers and farm owners’ families constituted the population for the study. A sample of hundred and twenty (120) respondents was drawn from the seven local government areas that formed the study area, and were administered questionnaire items. Data collected were analyzed using descriptive statistics and inferential analyses, including chi-squares tests and independent sample t-tests at 0.05 level of significance. The result revealed the socioeconomic characteristics, common associated hazards and health problems experience by the respondents. Economically exposed respondents lost greatly more income due to illness less than their non-exposed counterparts (t = 5.87, p<0.05). Significantly safety training was greatly associated with Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) usage (𝑥2 =21.54, p<0.05). The study concludes that pig production in the study area poses substantial occupational health and economic risks. The research recommends among others regular training on safety and zoonosis prevention, sensitization of farmers on safe handling practices and farm hygiene, enaction of policies supporting occupational health surveillance, and establishment of rural health clinics and mobile health outreach for pig farmers.

Occupational Health, Safety and Environmental (OHSE) compliance is a dynamic requirement for ensuring wellbeing, safety at work environments, curtailing work-related hazards and reassuring sustainable institutional procedures. This research evaluates the quality of OHSE compliance and its effects at Federal Polytechnic Bauchi, Nigeria. The study method adopted a cast study involving structured questionnaires, workplace adherences and inspection of safety-related documents. The study emphasized on safety observances, hazard regulatory procedures, personal protective equipment accessibility, emergency enthusiasm and environmental management routines. The findings demonstrate that effective OHSE compliance contributes significantly to accident prevention, better productivity, environmental safety and enhanced institutional sustainability. However, problems such as inadequate safety mindfulness, incoherent monitoring, inadequate safety resources and weak enforcement methods negate full compliance. The research recommends continuous safety training, enhanced inspection protocols, adequate provision of safety facilities (PPE), better-quality waste control systems and stronger institutional OHSE policies to intensify workshop safety and routine.

Criminal investigators face chronic demands beyond general police work: repeated analysis of traumatic digital evidence, heavy caseloads, cognitive overload, evidentiary scrutiny, and accountability for error (Schlosser et al., 2024;Strickland et al., 2023;Woodhams and Duran, 2024).Digitalization and rapidly changing technical requirements intensify these pressures while recruitment and retention problems restrict capacity (Drew et al., 2024). Burnout consequently threatens both officer well-being and investigative quality (Bezie et al., 2024).The literature separates operational stressors, which are intrinsic to the work, from organizational stressors, which arise from how the institution is run, such as workload allocation, supervisory support, role clarity, and culture (Gavin and Porter, 2024). A finding that is decisive for training design is that organizational and operational stressors, rather than trauma exposure alone, predict most stressrelated outcomes among investigative and forensic staff (Keech and Drew, 2026;Porter and Gavin, 2025). Among United States investigators exposed to CSAM, the frequency of exposure was not systematically related to mental health, apart from violent material, which was linked to elevated posttraumatic stress; agency-level factors such as control over workload, debriefing, and feedback on case outcomes were what mitigated harm (Mitchell et al., 2023). This Opinion draws on peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026, identified through database searches on police and investigator occupational stress, psychological capital, technostress, and organizational interventions, prioritizing evidence specific to investigative and forensic roles and using the broader occupational-health literature where role-specific studies are scarce. On that basis, I argue that stress-management interventions for investigators should rest on two complementary pillars. Operational training strengthens the adaptive capacity of the individual officer; organizational training reshapes the leadership, climate, and work systems in which officers operate (Figure 1). Current practice still leans heavily toward the first pillar, locating both the problem and its remedy in the worker. I treat investigator resilience as a structurally enabled resource rather than a fixed personal trait. The evidence supports a structural rather than an episodic framing. Multidimensional assessments show that police stress tracks enduring features of the work environment, including job demands, control, support, role clarity, and organizational change, more than isolated critical incidents (Strukcinskiene et al., 2025). Within investigative and forensic units, organizational and operational demands, not trauma exposure alone, predict the largest share of stress-related outcomes, while supervisor support, peer support, and a positive psychosocial safety climate act as the main buffering resources (Keech and Drew, 2026). This pattern recasts exposure as one demand among several rather than the sole cause of harm (Drew et al., 2024).The job demands-resources (JD-R) model explains how demands deplete well-being unless balanced by resources. Conservation of resources (COR) theory explains how continued depletion without recovery creates loss spirals and burnout (Demerouti et al., 2001;Hobfoll, 1989;Zhou et al., 2024). Operational training adds personal resources; organizational action protects them.Integration requires a multilevel and temporal account. Structural demands such as backlog, traumatic exposure, digital overload and ambiguity first activate the JD-R health-impairment pathway. The two pillars then operate in a reciprocal cycle: operational training may improve immediate regulation, appraisal and help-seeking, while organizational training changes workload, supervisory behaviour, recovery opportunities and psychological safety. These organizational changes determine whether personal gains are replenished or progressively depleted. COR theory therefore predicts that operational training is most useful during acute demand, whereas organizational redesign becomes increasingly important when demands are recurrent, controllable and system-generated. Professional identity is proposed as a mediator, not a presumed protection: stress may weaken identification through cynicism and perceived value conflict, while credible supervision and meaningful feedback may restore identification and its wellbeing benefits. Job security is proposed as a moderator because officers who fear transfer, stigma, career penalty or job loss may be less able to disclose strain or use support. The model predicts that combined interventions will be more durable when workload control, psychological safety and leadership accountability improve; it does not assume that combined interventions will always outperform individual training.Digital transformation adds a further, persistent demand. Technostress, the strain from constant connectivity, information overload, and the intrusion of technology into recovery time, behaves as a chronic job demand associated with lower well-being and burnout, and it is intrinsic to investigative work built around digital evidence (Pansini et al., 2023;Mansuroğlu and Smith, 2026). Two resources deserve emphasis because they locate where interventions should act. Professional identity mediates the link between occupational stress and well-being, and perceived job security moderates it, which indicates that meaning and stability are protective resources shaped largely by organizations rather than by individuals alone (Wu et al., 2025).Operational training targets the officer's own coping repertoire and has a credible evidence base.Mindfulness-based resilience training has shown feasibility and promising effects on stress in police samples (Christopher et al., 2024), and physiologically grounded programs that pair heart-ratevariability biofeedback with metacognitive skill practice are being trialed to build resilience in officers exposed to post-traumatic stress injuries (Andersen et al., 2023). These approaches develop psychological capital, the malleable resources of hope, efficacy, resilience, and optimism that are associated with lower burnout and turnover intention and with higher engagement and performance (Loghman et al., 2023).The limits of a purely individual approach are equally clear, and they should be stated without overclaiming the alternative. Worker-directed interventions place the burden of adaptation on the person, can imply that distress signals personal weakness, and tend to fade once officers return to unchanged conditions. They do not remediate the organizational stressors that the investigatorspecific evidence identifies as the deepest sources of harm (Gavin and Porter, 2024;Mitchell et al., 2023). Teaching investigators to regulate their physiology is useful, but it does not reduce an unmanageable caseload or a dismissive command climate.Comparative reviews suggest that organizational and combined interventions may produce benefits comparable with, and sometimes more durable than, individual interventions in healthcare and general workplaces (Catapano et al., 2023;Dahlqvist et al., 2023). This evidence cannot be treated as direct proof for investigative policing. Its relevance is theoretical and conditional: reducing demands at source should protect recovery, but policing adds hierarchy, operational urgency, confidentiality requirements and occupational stigma. Accordingly, the present framework offers a testable proposition rather than an effectiveness claim. Organizational action should be staged according to readiness, fidelity, leadership commitment and resources, with individual training retained as an accessible component while system-level effects are evaluated.For investigative units, this pillar includes trauma-informed supervision, case-outcome feedback, exposure and caseload review, breaks and recovery after graphic-material work, peer support, psychosocial safety monitoring, and leadership accountability (Mitchell et al., 2022(Mitchell et al., , 2023;;Keech and Drew, 2026). Leadership links the pillars because supportive leadership can strengthen psychological capital (Loghman et al., 2023). Table 1 distinguishes evidence from proposals requiring testing.Delivery should fit agency capacity. National laboratories may use exposure logging, specialist supervision, and rotation; small or rural forces may need regional case-sharing, remote consultation, peer supervision, and referral agreements. Internet-crime task forces may prioritize graphicexposure limits and outcome feedback, while general detective units address backlog, autonomy, and recovery. In lower-resource settings, feasible minimums include workload review, supervisor training, confidential referral, and protected recovery. The functions are transferable, but implementation must reflect staffing, geography, labor protections, culture, and stigma.Implementation barriers require active design responses. Hierarchy can be addressed through confidential reporting routes, supervisor accountability and protected escalation pathways; resource constraints through phased implementation and regional/shared services; stigma through routine, universal wellbeing processes rather than exceptional referral; confidentiality concerns through independent providers and clear data-governance rules; and competing priorities through integrating recovery, exposure review and case-outcome feedback into existing quality and supervision meetings.These strategies are proposed implementation mechanisms, not evidence of established effectiveness. Their value should be assessed using reach, fidelity, acceptability, equity of access and unintended-consequence indicators. Treating barriers as design conditions preserves the structural argument while acknowledging that organizational interventions can fail or impose new burdens if poorly implemented.Table 1. Evidence-calibrated intervention matrix. Indicators are proposed evaluation measures unless directly tested in the cited studies.Equity is a design requirement rather than a descriptive add-on. Access to resilience resources may vary by gender, rank, rurality, contract status, unit type and national capacity (Bezie et al., 2024;Porter and Gavin, 2025). Women officers may encounter additional caregiving demands, gendered expectations or lower psychological safety; junior officers may have less discretion to request recovery; rural officers may face distance, limited specialist services and confidentiality concerns in small teams. These conditions may alter both exposure to demands and the feasibility of each intervention. Implementation should therefore require disaggregated monitoring of reach, uptake, workload relief, perceived safety and outcomes by gender, rank, rurality and unit. Agencies should offer multiple access routes, remote and regional options, protected time, culturally appropriate providers and safeguards against career penalties. Core functions should be retained, but delivery should be adapted and tested rather than assumed to be equivalent across contexts.The pillars are complementary but not interchangeable. Policy should become auditable and equitable. Units should review caseload and graphic exposure regularly; provide confidential, trauma-informed supervision; record access to case-outcome feedback; protect recovery; and monitor climate, absence, turnover intention and support uptake. Universal exposure caps are premature. Agencies should instead define local trigger points for mandatory workload review, document exceptions and test whether thresholds predict health and service outcomes. Senior leaders should be accountable for system indicators alongside case throughput. Every implementation should report reach and effects by gender, rank, rurality, unit type and national context, and should include safeguards against retaliation, disclosure of sensitive case information and unequal access. Where resources are limited, minimum standards should include workload review, trained supervision, confidential referral and protected recovery time, with regional partnerships used to extend specialist access.The framework remains an evidence-informed working hypothesis. Investigator-specific studies identify plausible risks and protective practices, but causal evidence for organizational redesign is limited and evidence from other occupations is not automatically transferable. Agencies should therefore build officer skills, reduce recurrent resource depletion, and evaluate both workforce and investigative outcomes.

This study reconceptualizes organizational performance through the lens of systems thinking, arguing that conventional financial and efficiency-based approaches are increasingly inadequate for capturing the complexity of contemporary organizations. In response, this study develops a systemic conceptualization of performance as a multidimensional and emergent construct. Drawing on classical and contemporary contributions to systems theory, the analysis conceptualizes the organization as a complex sociotechnical system composed of interdependent subsystems embedded within dynamic environments. Within this framework, performance is not treated as a static outcome but as a dynamic property emerging from continuous interactions between internal structures and external conditions. This article examines the evolution of performance theories, from traditional financial models to multidimensional frameworks such as the Competing Values Framework, and discusses contemporary measurement approaches, including the Balanced Scorecard and sustainability-oriented frameworks. It ultimately proposes a systemic conception of performance structured around a viability-performance matrix, emphasizing feedback loops, adaptive capacity, and structural tensions between stability and flexibility. This study contributes to management theory by bridging systems thinking and performance literature, with implications for organizational design, governance, and sustainability-oriented management.

Some distribution networks are characterized by weak grid structures and complex feeder deployment, which leads to missing information such as line parameters. Existing power flow methods depend heavily on accurate parameters and lack sufficient dynamic adaptability, making them unsuitable for incomplete-information conditions. To address this problem, this paper proposes a distribution-network situation-awareness model driven by data-physical fusion. First, to cope with the dual challenges of incompleteness and uncertainty in line parameters, a bounded multi-operating-condition line-parameter identification model is constructed, and the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy is employed to determine line resistances and reactances; the resulting parameters are then used for data augmentation. Next, a situation-awareness model for distribution networks is developed by combining a physics-informed neural network with a mixture-of-experts architecture. In this way, data-driven learning is integrated with physical constraints so that the perceptual capability of deep learning is preserved while the model remains guided by power-flow physics. Finally, the model is validated using the IEEE 33-bus system and historical operating data from an actual distribution area in China. The results show that the proposed model outperforms the comparison methods on the IEEE 33-bus system and effectively tracks multiple state variables in the actual distribution area, supporting its feasibility for incomplete-information conditions.

Proper solid waste disposal is vital for public and environmental health, and waste collectors play a central role in maintaining community sanitation. Solid waste collectors experience high rates of injuries such as cuts and musculoskeletal disorders in Africa, largely due to inadequate PPE, poor training, and limited healthcare access. This study is significant because it fills the gap in community-level data on physical and psychosocial occupational hazards among solid waste collectors in Swali, Yenagoa, and providing evidence to improve occupational health and safety practices. The aim of this study was to assess the physical and psychosocial occupational hazards among waste collectors in Swali Community, Yenagoa, Bayelsa State. This research adopted a cross-sectional survey design. The target population comprised of all formal waste collectors in the Swali community who were exposed to physical and psychosocial occupational hazards. A total of 125 waste collectors were selected using a simple random sampling technique. Data was collected through structured questionnaire and observational checklist over a period of seven (7) weeks and analyzed using descriptive statistics with the aid of SPSS version 25. Findings revealed that the most frequently reported physical occupational hazard was cuts or puncture wounds with 44.8% of respondents agreeing and 24.0% strongly agreeing, yielding the highest mean score of 3.67 ± 1.18. Regarding psychosocial hazards, 52% reported experiencing stress due to your job, while 51% reported verbal abuse while working. In conclusion, the study found that waste collectors in Swali, Yenagoa, experience significant physical and psychosocial hazards. It is recommended that PPE compliance policies should be enforced and provision of safe work technique.

Wildfire research and management efforts have largely focused on fire suppression, risk assessment, and mitigation. Comparatively little attention has been given to post-wildfire reforestation, despite its potential influence on long-term forest recovery. To better understand post-wildfire restoration practices in Canada, national charity Forests Canada conducted a survey resulting in 80 responses from forest managers and tree planting practitioners. Forests Canada also conducted interviews with eight experts. The study examined decision-making processes guiding post-fire tree planting, operational practices used to promote successful forest establishment, and the extent to which future wildfire risk is considered during restoration planning. Results indicate that practitioners generally adopt a cautious and deliberate approach to post-wildfire reforestation. Key considerations include regeneration assessments, resource availability, regulatory requirements, environmental and wildlife values, community priorities, and site accessibility. Respondents reported several adjustments to traditional reforestation practices, particularly regarding tree spacing, microsite selection, operational costs, occupational health and safety measures, and consideration of future fire risk. Changes in species selection, nursery stock types, and salvage logging practices were also reported, although less consistently. The study identifies seven priority knowledge gaps requiring further attention: reforestation prioritization, species selection, Indigenous stewardship pathways, tree planting standards, site preparation and salvage logging, the true costs of artificial regeneration, and occupational health and safety.

Monitoring and improving animal health and welfare is a pressing need. Technological advances are increasing our ability to do so in a range of settings but there are limited uses in experimental settings for less common model animals. Red foxes ( Vulpes vulpes ) are maintained by the French National Agency for Food, Environmental, and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES) for regulatory and research purposes, primarily related to its role as a European Union and French Reference Laboratory for rabies and Echinococcus spp., both serious zoonoses. In 2022, four foxes were surgically fitted with internal implants that recorded body temperature and activity levels and subsequently inoculated with rabies virus (RABV). As a proof of concept, we retrospectively tested the potential of these two variables to provide an early warning for the onset of rabies symptoms. To do so, we applied two anomaly detection algorithms (Shewhart and EWMA) with varying confidence levels individually to the two data sets from each fox and compared how early the different models could detect significant changes while limiting false alarms during the calibration period. We found that all the foxes significantly changed their activity during infection. We were best able to detect these changes at the individual fox level using the EWMA algorithm, in some cases producing consecutive alarms up to two weeks before the death of an animal, while limiting false alarms. We found no evidence of fever in any of the infected foxes and body temperature did not appear to be a reliable indicator of foxes’ health in this context. While here we applied our methods to a particularly severe and rarely implemented model with a limited sample size, this proof of concept illustrates the potential of these methods for a wide range of other situations that would benefit from similar long-term monitoring, including experimental protocols with milder clinical signs and routine monitoring for unexpected declines in health or welfare.

Introduction: Night work and extended work schedules are among the leading occupational health risk factors. Objectives: To estimate the prevalence of night work among the employed Brazilian population. Methods: Cross-sectional, population-based study using data from the 2019 Brazilian National Survey of Health. Individuals aged 15 years or older who belonged to the economically active employed population were included. The outcome was self-reported night work, assessed using a survey question on work performed between 8:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m. Responses were recorded as 0 = no and 1 = yes. Prevalence estimates and their 95% CIs were calculated accounting for the complex survey design according to sociodemographic, occupational, and state-level characteristics. Associations were evaluated using the Rao-Scott adjusted Pearson chi-square test. Results: The national prevalence of night work was 13.3% (95% CI, 12.8%-13.9%), ranging from 5.8% in Acre to 16.6% in Rio de Janeiro. Night work was more frequent in urban areas (14.2%), among men (16.3%), and among higher-income individuals (15.5%). The highest prevalences were observed in the accommodation and food services (28.7%) and transportation, warehousing, and postal services (26.9%) sectors. Conclusions: Approximately one in seven workers in Brazil engaged in night work. The prevalence varied according to regional, sociodemographic, and occupational characteristics, with higher prevalences in sectors requiring continuous operations. These findings underscore the importance of monitoring work schedules and implementing policies to protect the health of workers exposed to night work.

Wearable biometric systems increasingly support cognitive ergonomics and human-system interaction, forcing design-time trade-offs between physiological signal quality and data-protection requirements.This study presents a system-level framework for jointly assessing signal fidelity and privacy risk in multimodal wearable biometric systems.Using a public affective-physiology dataset of 32 participants, signals were processed into a signal-quality index that captures noise robustness, spectral complexity, artifact prevalence, and temporal stability.Privacy risk was quantified as the worst case across complementary attack vectors, namely re-identification, membership inference, and informationtheoretic leakage, so that a single high-risk channel rather than an averaged score governs the estimate.

A part of the difficulties encountered by primary school children in the training process is related to the instructional materials presented in textbooks. When instructional materials are not presented in accordance with pupils’ age-related, cognitive, emotional, volitional, and individual psychological characteristics, they place an additional cognitive load on perception, attention, memory, and thinking processes, make it more difficult to organize attention, and may lead to failure in learning activities, reduced cognitive engagement, lower self-confidence, and decreased learning motivation.

Purpose This study investigates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) implementation on healthcare professional role adaptation and training program effectiveness, examining the mediating roles of sociotechnical integration and professional attitudes towards AI. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 255 healthcare professionals in India, including physicians, nurses, paramedical, and support staff from various facility types. The study employed a quantitative approach using validated scales to measure AI Technology Implementation, Sociotechnical Integration, Professional Attitudes towards AI, Professional Role Adaptation, and Training Program Effectiveness. Findings AI implementation had significant positive total effects on both professional role adaptation and training program effectiveness. These effects were partially mediated by sociotechnical integration and professional attitudes towards AI: both mediators transmitted a significant positive indirect effect from AI implementation to each outcome, while the direct effects remained positive and significant. Sociotechnical integration was the stronger mediator, particularly for training program effectiveness. The effects varied across different healthcare roles and facility types. Practical implications The findings emphasize the need for healthcare organizations to foster positive attitudes towards AI among staff, ensure thorough sociotechnical integration, and develop tailored, context-sensitive approaches to AI implementation and training programs. Originality/value This study provides a detailed, empirically grounded account of AI adoption in healthcare, showing that the benefits of AI implementation for professional roles and training are channelled through social and organizational factors rather than arising from technology alone. It highlights the critical importance of human factors and organizational context in shaping AI implementation outcomes, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of technological change in healthcare settings.

documents.abstract: The Office Ergonomics Research Committee (OERC) is an industry research consortium consisting of companies that collaborate to advance ergonomics/human factors research in the design and management of knowledge workplaces, systems, processes, and products. OERC members represent a diverse group of organizations with a common interest in complex human-computer technology systems, namely, office ergonomics. Members of OERC seek to expand their understanding of the human-technology system in office settings through sponsored research by partnering with university researchers to advance knowledge in human factors/ergonomics. OERC has funded research projects that explore novel approaches, address underexplored challenges, and generate research with actionable insights that support healthier, more productive, and equitable office environments for over 35 years. This panel comprises OERC members and previously OERC-funded university researchers, who will present highlights and reflections on their academic research projects as well as the benefits and roles of OERC membership.

This study explored the predictive role of responsive digital pedagogy in shaping elementary learner engagement in Baggao, Cagayan. It focused on four dimensions of digital teaching: adaptive digital task design, responsive feedback, participatory digital interaction, and access-sensitive instructional support. An explanatory-predictive path design was applied to data from 90 public elementary school teachers selected through stratified criterion-random sampling. Responses were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, bootstrapping with 10,000 resamples, PLSpredict, and importance-performance map analysis. The measurement model established acceptable reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Results showed that responsive digital pedagogy explained 62.4% of the variance in learner engagement. Responsive feedback exerted the strongest positive effect, followed by participatory digital interaction and adaptive digital task design. Access-sensitive instructional support, however, did not significantly predict engagement and emerged as the weakest area of implementation. Predictive analysis further showed that the model performed better in explaining active participation, sustained attention, and learning effort than cognitive involvement. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of digital instruction depends less on technology use itself and more on how teachers adapt digital experiences, provide timely feedback, and create meaningful opportunities for participation. Strengthening access-sensitive practices and designing tasks that promote deeper cognitive engagement are recommended to improve responsive digital teaching in elementary classrooms.

Abstract As flow chemistry emerges as a pivotal technology for achieving sustainable development goals (SDGs), integrating it into the undergraduate curriculum requires an understanding of the total student experience. This study applies Novak’s theory of meaningful learning to evaluate the cognitive, affective, and psychomotor experiences of 82 students in a green flow chemistry laboratory. Data from a 15-item Likert survey and open-ended responses reveal a strikingly asymmetric learning profile: while students reported high cognitive engagement (mean = 4.30) and strong intrigue with the equipment (mean = 4.49), their psychomotor confidence was markedly lower (mean = 3.60). Notably, students expressed high attraction to the equipment (positive affect) alongside persistent intimidation and low confidence in data-driven decision-making (psychomotor). These results suggest that while green chemistry principles serve as effective cognitive and affective anchors for student interest, the technical novelty of flow systems creates a psychomotor threshold that current single-session formats do not fully bridge. Our findings demonstrate that measuring only cognition and affect would obscure this bottleneck, underscoring the importance of independently assessing all three domains. We propose that prelab familiarization activities, distributed multisession exposure, and explicit linking of experimental steps to green chemistry principles can support the development of technically confident sustainable chemists.

The article discusses and justifies the application motivational exercises at the adaptation stage in professionally-oriented foreign-language training for undergraduate students at a technical university. The purpose of the article is to substantiate and experimentally confirm the effectiveness of integration motivational exercises at the adaptation stage in foreign-language training of students. The article notes that senior students who possess a high level of lexical competence in the terminology of a specific scientific field nonetheless have difficulty while confronted with the need to use interdisciplinary information in a foreign language, which requires the ability to interpret such information. The article presents a specially designed set of motivational exercises: training drills, ice-breakers, profession-focused communicative exercises, and developmental tasks. The methodology includes an analysis of scientific papers on the study of exercises in foreign language learning, integration of an adaptation stage into academic programs, diagnosis of personal characteristics and linguоcognitive abilities of students. The experiment demonstrated that an adaptation stage with exercises in predictive thinking and creativity (including elements of science fiction and artificial language) increases students’ readiness to innovation in a scientific environment. The results confirmed a statistically significant reduction of language anxiety by 29.01%, an increase in intrinsic motivation by 23.39% and rates of development of probabilistic forecasting by 27.87%, verbal creativity by 29.61%. Motivational exercises at the adaptation stage in professionally-oriented foreign language training of senior technical university students create an adaptive educational environment: it reduces language barriers; enhances intrinsic motivation; develops soft and cognitive skills and also dynamically adjusts the content and educational trajectory based on the results of continuous diagnosis.

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital platform work has transformed how labour is organized, evaluated, and compensated, deepening workers' dependence on technology-mediated systems. This integrative literature review examines the relationship between technostress and worker well-being in the platform economy, with particular attention to algorithmic management. Drawing on 29 peer-reviewed sources identified through a structured search of academic databases and search engines, the review synthesizes evidence on techno-overload, techno-complexity, techno-insecurity, and techno-uncertainty alongside algorithmic monitoring, performance evaluation, scheduling, and compensation. Technology-related demands are consistently associated with emotional exhaustion, poorer well-being, work–life conflict, burnout, impaired productivity, reduced engagement, and intentions to discontinue platform work. These relationships are not uniform: worker appraisal, self-efficacy, personality, autonomy, transparency, fairness, and human influence shape how technological demands are experienced, while economic dependence and financial insecurity can intensify the consequences of algorithmic control by limiting workers' ability to reject undesirable conditions or exit platforms. The review conceptualizes platform worker well-being as a sociotechnical outcome arising from the interaction of digital demands, algorithmic governance, individual resources, and structural conditions, and proposes an integrated multilevel framework linking these elements. Gaps concerning longitudinal evidence, cross-platform comparison, measurement integration, geographic diversity, and platform-level interventions are identified, and a corresponding research agenda is outlined. The review contributes by connecting technostress theory with algorithmic-management and platform-dependence perspectives, and by arguing that improving platform worker well-being requires attention to platform design and governance rather than individual coping alone.

Scholars and practitioners alike have long presumed that power and status, two foundational bases of social hierarchy, share a symmetric, mutually reinforcing relationship. However, support for this presumption has largely taken the form of theoretical accounts due to the prevalence of static research designs and a dearth of dynamic methodology in organizational research. Drawing on the Dual Perspective Model, we propose that one’s status is more likely to drive changes in one’s power than vice versa because status has a stronger connection to communion—an important component of interpersonal evaluations—than does power, and communality is an important predictor of both power and status. Using data from two studies involving project teams and a contemporary methodology from developmental psychology for modeling dynamic relationships (bivariate dual change score models), we illustrate that there is indeed a mutually reinforcing relationship between power and status over time, but this relationship is asymmetric. In three additional experiments, we find that perceptions of communality explain this asymmetry. We also find similar effects whether power is formal—attached to a position or role—or involves control over informal resources. Across all studies, we find that the path from status to changes in power is stronger than the path from power to changes in status.

Abstract Functional ideation in systemic design unfolds within sociotechnical and sociocultural environments where goals, constraints, and evaluative criteria evolve across multiple levels of organization. Creativity research explains important aspects of novelty, variation, recombination, and selective retention, but it often treats novelty as emerging within a relatively stable representational space or a single level of abstraction. Systemic design scholarship, in turn, has developed strong approaches for framing complexity, mapping relations, organizing participation, and coordinating action, but it less often specifies how designers navigate between systemic levels, address challenges at different levels of abstraction, and construct intervention candidates while the task environment is still being differentiated. This paper responds by proposing a naturalistic framework of ideation within the Interactivist–Constructivist paradigm, with the IDEA Design Scaffold as its methodological architecture for systemic design. The central claim is that functional ideation under systemic complexity must be understood as a self-directed developmental process: intervention opportunities become novel and appropriate as designers navigate across levels of complexity through anticipatory exploration, partial stabilization, reflective reorganization, and rebuilding of missing supports. IDEAS operationalizes this account by linking Systemic Breakdown and Systemic Integration through the Iterative Innovation Cycle, enabling systemic goals, design challenges, and intervention candidates to be progressively coordinated without reducing ideation to a fixed procedure. The payoff is both theoretical and methodological: the paper explains why creative development in systemic design requires movement across levels of complexity, and provides an architecture for supporting, studying, and refining that movement in systemic design practice.

documents.abstract: Lexical borrowing has become a common phenomenon in English language learning. However, its psychological influence on young EFL learners remains underexplored, particularly regarding how borrowed words may relate to classroom engagement. Previous studies have examined lexical borrowing from linguistic and cognitive perspectives; however, little attention has been paid to its psychological and pedagogical implications in elementary school contexts. This study investigates students’ awareness of the borrowed word insecure and its role in shaping classroom engagement at MI Khadijah Malang. Employing a qualitative case study approach, the research involved 21 students from Grades Four, Five, and Six. Data were collected through classroom observations and semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal that students demonstrated different levels of awareness of the borrowed word insecure, with their understanding developing through exposure to English instruction, social media, peer interaction, and other everyday social environments. Students interpreted the term not only as an expression of low self-confidence but also as a reflection of academic comparison, anxiety, and self-improvement. Furthermore, the borrowed word was internalized in three distinct ways: as a source of motivation, as a form of self-doubt, and as having limited psychological influence. Interview and observation data showed that some students who associated insecure with self-improvement became more motivated, increased their learning effort, or developed new learning strategies, such as learning through songs, increasing vocabulary exposure, and using language-learning applications. In contrast, some students who compared themselves with higher-achieving peers experienced self-doubt and showed reduced participation or motivation, while others reported little influence from the term and maintained stable classroom participation. These different interpretations were associated with varying patterns of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement in the English classroom. The study concludes that the relationship between the borrowed word insecure and classroom engagement is not uniform but varies according to how learners internalize and relate its meaning to their academic experiences and social interactions. By integrating lexical borrowing with learner engagement theory, this study demonstrates that borrowed words may function not only as linguistic resources but also as psychological labels that are associated with learners’ engagement in English language learning.

Labor compliance with the use of personal protective equipment can reduce the chances of work accidents and work-related diseases. In the industrial sector, it can be seen that many workers are reluctant or even not wearing PPE at all, this is due to several factors such as comfort, discomfort is one of the main reasons why workers do not use PPE according to standards, both in duration and how to use. This study aims to determine the relationship between the comfort of personal protective equipment (PPE) and compliance with the use of PPE in PT Tasma Puja workers in 2025. The research method used an observational analytical design with a cross sectional approach on 119 respondents from a population of 170 harvesters using simple random sampling. Data collection was carried out through a questionnaire and analyzed using the Chi-Square test. The results showed that there was a significant relationship between comfort and compliance with the use of PPE with a p value of 0.000. Most of the respondents are non-compliant and uncomfortable using PPE, so the lower the compliance of workers. The conclusion of this study shows that the comfort of PPE plays an important role in increasing worker compliance so that companies need to pay attention to ergonomics, quality, and comfort factors of PPE so that work safety increases and the number of work accidents in oil palm plantations can be reduced sustainably in the future. It is recommended that companies increase routine supervision and the application of sanctions and awards for workers, in order to increase the discipline of PPE use

documents.abstract: As the global manufacturing landscape undergoes rapid transformation, organizations are compelled to enhance productivity, reduce waste, and strengthen competitiveness. Lean manufacturing has emerged as a critical methodology to achieve these objectives, fundamentally shifting how businesses approach production by eliminating non-value-adding activities, pursuing continuous improvement, and utilizing resources efficiently. Within this paradigm, the design of plant layouts plays a pivotal role, serving as the foundation for operational efficiency through optimized workflow, reduced transportation, and effective space utilization. This review paper examines the multifaceted relationship between plant layout and lean manufacturing, tracing its evolution from the Toyota Production System to contemporary Industry 4.0-enabled smart factories. The paper explores foundational lean principles, various layout typologies, integration with lean tools such as 5S, Kaizen, and Kanban, and the emerging influence of digital technologies including digital twins, the Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence. Furthermore, it addresses human factors and ergonomics, environmental sustainability through green lean approaches, sector-specific applications, and persistent implementation challenges. By synthesizing insights from academic literature and industry case studies, this paper provides a strategic framework for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to leverage layout design as a driver of lean transformation and long-term operational excellence.

Background Normalization of Deviance (NoD) is a well-documented organizational failure mode in aviation, yet its propagation through digital ecosystems remains unexplored. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) highlights a critical mentorship vacuum due to pilot retirements, and social media platforms increasingly serve as informal training environments. This study introduces the concept of Algorithmic Normalization of Deviance- ANoD, hypothesizing that recommendation algorithms systematically reward and amplify “gray-zone” cockpit behaviors that erode sterile flight deck protocols. Method We conducted a stratified netnographic analysis of 150 high-visibility aviation videos (N = 150) across Instagram Reels, split between algorithmically recommended content (n = 100) and curated influencer content (n = 50). A novel coding framework operationalized compliance (Compliant vs. Gray Zone vs. Deviant) and incentive structures. Engagement metrics were analyzed to quantify the algorithmic advantage of non-compliant behavior. Results The analysis reveals a directionally consistent “Viral Deviation” pattern rather than a statistically decisive one. Gray-zone recordings (i.e., technically legal but procedurally borderline) comprised 57% of the sample and attracted higher engagement than compliant content, although this difference was small and did not reach conventional significance (d = 0.24, p = 0.11). The clearest signal emerged between content sources: algorithmically surfaced posts showed significantly higher interaction rates than curated influencer posts (d = 0.31, p = 0.029), a small but statistically significant per-view advantage for content promoted directly by the recommendation system. Structural incentive analysis further indicates that monetization pressures co-occur with increased gray-zone production, structurally analogous to a parallel, shadow curriculum associated with conditions that may facilitate drift. Conclusion The study identifies statistical associations, not causal relationships, and the downstream behavioural impact on pilots is hypothesised from the algorithmic-pattern evidence rather than directly measured. Within those bounds, social media algorithms constitute a structurally unmonitored distribution channel whose observed associations with gray-zone content amplification are consistent with a normalisation-of-deviance feedback mechanism operating beyond current regulatory oversight — an association that warrants urgent empirical validation and proactive governance. We propose a shift from prohibition to risk-stratified governance, recommending that regulators distinguish between handheld (high-risk) and mounted (managed-risk) devices, and integrate digital algorithmic literacy into ab-initio pilot training to counter this new systemic threat.

ABSTRACT There have been emerging media reports on the impact of cyanide and mercury use in artisanal and small‐scale gold mining (ASGM) operations on community health, especially among pregnant and non‐pregnant women, ASGM miners, and children in rural Africa. This paper gathers data from multiple sources, including media reports and qualitative research interviews, to critically examine and question the emerging environmental and public health concerns of ASGM operations in rural Africa, using Ghana, a country that has experienced a surge in illegal/informal mining activities over the past two decades, as a case study. Our findings revealed multifaceted and interrelated factors comprising (i) community exposure to heavy metals and disease contraction, (ii) congenital disabilities and pregnant women's exposure to toxic chemicals from ASGM operations, (iii) miners' exposure, disease burden and ill health, (iv) water‐related diseases, and (v) heavy metal bioaccumulation in food chains and associated with public health risks, as the growing environmental and public health risks and concerns of ASGM operations in Ghana. Based on these findings, we suggest a multidisciplinary socio‐ecological policy approach to mitigate the environmental risks and health concerns associated with ASGM operations in Ghana and, more broadly, across Africa. In this context, an integrated One Health approach that focuses on ASGM regulations, environmental management, occupational health and safety, public health, stakeholder engagement and community participation can be considered a suitable multidisciplinary socio‐ecological policy response. The policy and practical implications of our findings are discussed in the paper.

This article examines the turnover of agricultural land plots in the context of the digitalization of public administration. It has been established that the management of land plots is not keeping pace with the rapid development of the digitalization of public administration; consequently, there is a need to improve the legislation governing the civil circulation of these plots. Issues related to the turnover of agricultural land remain relevant because proper regulation of this process allows for the optimization of relations between landowners, users, other individuals, local government bodies, and the state. The development of digital technologies in the field of public administration, on the one hand, allows for simplifying the process of land resource management; on the other hand, it requires additional measures from the state to ensure the proper protection of registries, the personal information of registry users, their uninterrupted operation, and so on. Taking into account the research conducted on the outlined issues concerning the management of agricultural land plots and the development of judicial practice in this area, the chosen field of study becomes a subject of both scientific and practical interest, and the development of proposals to improve the existing mechanism requires a balanced and comprehensively justified approach, since, as experience has shown, the digital technology sector is no less vulnerable to the human factor than the system currently in operation. The study found that current legislation needs to be updated to incorporate the latest advances in the digitization of public administration. When dealing with land plots in general and agricultural land plots in particular, digital technologies should be actively utilized to ensure the performance of all registration, analytical, monitoring, and other activities; to this end, appropriate amendments must be made to current legislation. The author’s vision for the implementation of mechanisms for the digitalization of public administration in the management of agricultural land is presented.

Background: According to human-centered design principles, user experience and user satisfaction are key aspects when developing or providing patients and clients with assistive, rehabilitation, or training technologies. Existing tools for assessing user experience and satisfaction are often either too narrow (developed for specific technologies) or too broad, failing to capture all relevant aspects of the technology being evaluated. Objective: The main objective of this study was to present the development process and content validation of a questionnaire that, following further validation steps, could be useful for researchers and developers in assessing the satisfaction of direct end users with assistive, rehabilitation, and training technologies. Methods: The development of the User Satisfaction Questionnaire for Assistive, Rehabilitation, and Training Technologies (U-ART-Q) followed a multistep process: (1) literature review, (2) domain definition and item generation, (3) expert consultation, (4) linguistic validation, and (5) content validation. Initially, 72 items were generated and organized into 7 domains. After expert review and linguistic validation, the questionnaire underwent content validation by 8 experts in physiotherapy, kinesiology, and ergonomics. Each item was rated for relevance using a 4-point Likert-type scale. The content validity ratio (CVR) and item-level content validity index (I-CVI) were calculated, and items below the accepted thresholds were removed or further revised. Results: Expert consultation resulted in the removal or merging of 20 items to improve clarity and reduce redundancy. Of the 52 items evaluated during content validation, 44 met the CVR and I-CVI criteria (CVR >0.75 and I-CVI >0.78). Eight items required additional review, and 2 items were ultimately removed. The final questionnaire comprises 10 initial screening questions and 50 content-valid items across 7 domains: design, comfort, effectiveness and usefulness, service, treatment or exercise, overall impressions, and safety. The overall average content validity index was 0.915, providing evidence of strong content validity. A macro-enabled Excel tool was developed to automate item selection and generate a PDF version of the questionnaire based on initial screening responses. Conclusions: The U-ART-Q is a newly developed instrument for assessing user satisfaction with assistive, rehabilitation, and training technologies. Further research will focus on psychometric evaluation, reliability testing, and multilingual validation to determine whether the U-ART-Q can provide a standardized method for assessing user satisfaction. Once fully evaluated, the questionnaire could support both developmental usability testing and postmarket evaluation, facilitating evidence-based decision-making and guiding future product improvement.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based chatbots offer new methodological opportunities for psychological research by enabling scalable, standardised, and interactive research procedures. However, their usefulness depends on the researchers’ ability to customise, evaluate, and deploy them in ways that align with the methodological requirements of a given study. The current tutorial provides a practical, step-by-step framework for developing customised LLM-based chatbots for psychological research. We distinguish between no-code or low-code development approaches, including provider-hosted chatbot builders and visual or low-code programming platforms, and code-based approaches using proprietary model application programming interfaces (APIs) or locally hosted open-weight models. We compare these approaches in terms of technical expertise, behavioural and workflow control, study integration, cost, data governance, maintenance, and reproducibility. We also outline key components of the process of customising an LLM-based chatbot and illustrate deployment workflows across multiple platforms, including local desktop interfaces, messaging applications and survey platforms. Finally, we discuss key considerations for research ethics, privacy, data governance, security, transparency, and reproducibility, including recommendations for documenting and sharing chatbot configurations and study procedures. Through this tutorial, we aim to support researchers in integrating customised LLM-based chatbots into psychological research and in expanding the methodological possibilities available to them.

documents.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used to support physical and mental health interventions. Recently, VR combined with hypnotic suggestions, termed virtual reality hypnosis (VRH), has emerged as a promising approach across clinical and non-clinical settings. This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the use and effectiveness of VRH. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO, and Embase following PRISMA guidelines. A total of 54 studies involving healthy and clinical populations were included. Meta-analytic results based on pre-post comparisons indicated a trend toward reduced anxiety following VRH (Hedges’ g = −1.39; 95% CI: −2.91 to 0.14). However, no significant differences were found when VRH was compared with other interventions, and no significant effects emerged for pain outcomes. Overall, VRH appears to be a promising intervention integrating immersive virtual environments with hypnotic suggestion, although further high-quality research is needed.

Hazardous materials (hazmat) road transportation entails substantial safety risks, in which driver-related factors are consistently identified as the leading contributors to crashes. Yet the occupational profile, health status, and psychosocial resources of hazmat truck drivers remain poorly characterized, constraining the development of evidence-based safety management. To address this gap, this study surveyed 347 hazmat truck drivers in China, combining standardized scales with self-developed items capturing context-specific working experiences. These drivers were middle-aged (M = 42.52 years). The majority of them (87.6%) were overweight or obese. More than half of them were suffering musculoskeletal discomfort (58.8%) and suspected insomnia or insomnia (56.8%) together with daytime sleepiness. Although their self-reported fatigue was relatively low, sleep-related problems and physical health issues warrant particular attention. Network analysis further revealed two functionally distinct clusters within the work system: a physiological risk cluster (fatigue, insomnia, and daytime sleepiness) and a psychosocial resource cluster (perceived social support, professional identity, and subjective well-being). The associations between the two clusters were predominantly negative, suggesting a dynamic balance between occupational strain and adaptive resources. Subjective well-being, insomnia, and fatigue emerged as the most central nodes, indicating that they may serve as priority entry points for intervention. Our findings highlight that safeguarding the occupational health and safety of hazmat truck drivers requires an integrated and system-oriented management approach that jointly addresses physiological risks, psychosocial resources, and physical health. The study offers empirical evidence and practical implications for safety management in hazmat road transportation.

Abstract Human error is a natural part of complex healthcare systems, including dentistry. Dental care combines diagnostic reasoning, procedures, medication management, radiographs, infection control, lab work, digital tools, and teamwork. Errors can happen due to individual mistakes, but also to problems with communication, systems, equipment, processes, or the work environment. Research on dental patient safety has identified issues such as diagnostic and treatment-planning errors, communication breakdowns, medication incidents, procedural complications, wrong-site or wrong-tooth treatments, foreign-body aspiration or swallowing, and documentation problems. Modern patient safety science now recommends moving away from blaming individuals and instead focusing on system-based human factors. This review covers the main types of human error in dental practice, such as slips, lapses, mistakes, violations, active errors, and hidden risks. It also looks at factors that contribute to errors, including cognitive, technical, communication, environmental, technological, organizational, and patient-related issues. Prevention strategies include using standard protocols, safety checklists, clear communication, double-checking diagnoses, medication reviews, simulation training, incident reporting, root cause analysis, teamwork, and building a fair safety culture. The Swiss Cheese Model helps explain how multiple weaknesses in safety barriers can align and cause harm to patients. In the end, making dentistry safer means not just relying on individuals to be careful but also designing systems that account for human limitations, catch errors, and support learning within the organization. Keywords: Human error; Human factors; Dental practice; Patient safety; Dental errors.

This study examines how Taiwanese parent-child families negotiate a "good" family life through everyday energy use and imagine future smart homes that support it. We conducted in-home interviews and co-design sessions with 21 families, including 46 parents and children. We found that families pursued a good life through energy practices shaped by thrift, comfort, care, safety, and enjoyment. These arrangements were continually adapted and responded to changing bodies, schedules, people, and infrastructures. This adaptive work was unevenly distributed, which in turn shaped different smart-home imaginaries. Drawing on the lens of Nearby and adversarial design, we conceptualize adaptation as situated sociotechnical work through which families continually rework energy arrangements. We further distinguish collective goods from plural and contestable goods to show why family IoT must support shared values while preserving opportunities to question and revise household arrangements. We offer theoretical and design directions for more adaptive, participatory, and contestable family IoT.

Abstract The Finite Sets Statistics-based Probability Hypothesis Density filter offers a description of a group of known or unknown targets as a single random entity with a Bayesian filtering framework. The Probability Hypothesis Density filter has often been employed in the Space Situational Awareness detection and tracking of space objects. One of its challenges is the determination of key probabilistic parameters, such as birth rates and birth intensities, for the detection of new space objects. Additionally, the challenge of incorporating nonlinear measurements requires the choice of simplifying assumptions on the prior, therefore introducing errors to the posterior. In this paper, a data-driven parameter flow version of the Probability Hypothesis Density filter is introduced, which performs the measurement update step using both birth and persistent likelihood densities while alleviating errors introduced to the posterior intensity. Therefore, preventing a shift of the birth intensity from the prediction step. A birth intensity is instantiated by performing a measurement correlation optimization, where the solution and likelihood are used to parametrize the intensity. In a data-driven discrete parameter flow Gaussian Mixture Probability Hypothesis Density filter implementation, the performance of the new birth is shown in a simulated ground-based optical tracking scenario. In optical tracking scenarios, tracklets composed of angles and angle rates are often assumed to be available. A multi-layer Probability Hypothesis Density filter is introduced, which forms tracklets before employing the full orbital data-driven Probability Hypothesis filter and the birth process. A Gaussian Mixture implementation of the multi-layer Probability Hypothesis filter is tested with a dataset for a GPS satellite collected from the Purdue Optical Ground Station.
topics: Target Tracking and Data Fusion in Sensor Networks

documents.abstract: To enhance laboratory safety, a risk assessment was conducted in environmental engineering laboratories using the Fine-Kinney Method (FKM) and Fault Tree Analysis (FTA). The FKM was initially employed to prioritize hazards, with a subsequent FTA used to systematically identify root causes and evaluate the effectiveness of existing controls. These two complementary approaches identified 10 risks, categorized into four groups: physical (electricity, fire, falling, sharp object injury), chemical (acid, poisoning, contamination), biological (infection, allergy), and ergonomic (musculoskeletal injury). Post-control measures successfully eliminated 89.3% of ‘Not Tolerated’ risks, contributing to an overall 63% reduction across all high-priority categories, including ‘Not Tolerated,’ ‘Strong,’ and ‘Important’ risks in FKM. Application of the FTA led to substantial risk reductions, with post-control measures decreasing hazard scores for fire, acid exposure, and electricity by 72.8%, 66.5%, and 60.0%, respectively. The statistical validation of the findings confirmed that the risk reductions achieved in both the FKM and FTA models were highly significant. The alignment of risk rankings across both models validated the assessment's reliability, providing a robust foundation for decision-making. Finally, implementing these validated safety measures requires a total budget of $42,000.

Large language model (LLM)-based clinical assistants are increasingly being integrated into electronic health record (EHR) systems, transforming how clinicians retrieve and synthesize information from patient records. Their safety and utility depend on rigorous evaluation, yet existing benchmarks are manually curated, costly to update, and rapidly become obsolete with evolving technological advancements. We present a scalable framework that automatically generates question--answer pairs from longitudinal EHR notes. Nineteen clinicians validate the benchmark generator, producing the Benchmark for Retrieving Information in EHRs (BRIE), a continuously maintainable evaluation dataset. Across nine LLMs and five inference strategies, state-of-the-art systems frequently omit clinically important information, particularly for questions requiring synthesis across multiple documents and encounters. Because the generator itself is validated, BRIE supports evaluations that static benchmarks cannot, including the generation of multiple answers that reflect variation in clinician reasoning for robust performance assessment and continuously refreshing benchmark content to guard against leakage. Our results demonstrate that scalable benchmark generation enables rigorous, up-to-date evaluation of clinical LLMs as they are deployed in rapidly evolving healthcare settings.

Against the backdrop of accelerating premiumization among Chinese new energy vehicle brands, an objective measurement method for perceived luxury has become a critical methodological challenge for the industry. This study conducts in-vehicle human factors experiments using Rolls-Royce, Voyah Dreamer, and Zunjie as test vehicles, investigating the neural cognitive mechanisms and quantitative evaluation methods of cabin luxury perception across five sensory dimensions: somatosensory, tactile, olfactory, auditory, and visual. The experiment collects electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG), electrodermal activity (EDA), skin temperature (SKT), and eye-tracking data, which are integrated with subjective evaluations for comprehensive analysis. Based on these findings, this paper establishes a four-dimensional quantitative evaluation framework encompassing physiological arousal, EEG processing, behavioral responses, and subjective ratings, and proposes a sensory consistency threshold model to explain the nonlinear integration mechanism underlying overall perceptions of luxury.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: The Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation and the screening practices built around it interpret lumbar injury risk primarily through axial compression, yet anterior–posterior shear is associated with injury at loads below established compressive thresholds. L4 and L5 as are henceforth defined as the 4th and 5th lumbar vertebrae Using a harmonized database of 106 peak-loading lifting postures reconstructed through digital human modeling across five studies, we developed parallel families of linear mixed-effects regression models for L4/L5 compression and shear that shared identical predictor sets and matched random-effects structures, isolating biomechanical differences from differences in statistical specification. Load magnitude and horizontal hand reach acted as universal drivers of both outcomes—positive, highly significant, and stable across model reduction—although compression was several times more sensitive in absolute terms. The two components diverged in their posture sensitivities: knee flexion was significant only for shear, whereas trunk flexion, shoulder flexion, and vertical hand position acted predominantly on compression. Critically, no predictor significant in both families reversed sign, indicating that posture selectively modulates two independently sourced quantities—the moment arm of the supported mass, which governs compression, and the orientation of the lumbar segment, which governs shear—rather than redistributing a single conserved spinal reaction. Between-subject variability consistently exceeded between-task variability and persisted across model reduction, identifying individual lifting strategy as a structural determinant of spinal exposure. Among the 102 observations below the 3.4 kN compression criterion, 11 (10.8%) exceeded the lower 700 N shear reference, although none exceeded the upper 1000 N reference. Together these findings give a quantitative rationale for regarding compression-only assessment as structurally incomplete and support a multidimensional, posture-aware approach to ergonomic risk evaluation.

Trustworthiness has become an important focus of artificial intelligence (AI) research. Although trustworthiness is a multifaceted concept and its requirements may depend on the context in which AI is used, little is known about how the public perceives these requirements. To address this issue, we conducted a questionnaire survey with nonexpert participants to examine the requirements that the public considers important for trustworthy AI and how their perceived value differs between social and nonsocial contexts. We further compared these context-dependent patterns with those observed for human trustworthiness. Our findings showed that, across social and nonsocial contexts, confidentiality and privacy protection were among the most important requirements for AI trustworthiness whereas the relative importance of other requirements depended on the context. In nonsocial contexts, transparency and interpretability of decision-making were particularly important whereas in social contexts, the ability to collaborate and communicate and a positive public image and attractive appearance were predominantly significant. Although similar context-dependent patterns were observed for human trustworthiness, findings consistently highlighted the ability to collaborate and communicate as a requirement for trusting humans, regardless of context, in contrast to AI trustworthiness. These findings provide insights into the public’s perception of trustworthy AI and highlight the importance of considering the context in which AI is used when examining AI trustworthiness requirements.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can turn learning analytics into personalized support, but feedback systems must decide when to intervene, which evidence to use, and how much assistance to provide. We developed a risk-adaptive, evidence-constrained framework for introductory programming using 2993 failed-submission states from 215 students. Student-disjoint models predicted persistent failure and related outcomes; four matched feedback conditions were generated for 136 cases; and calibrated risk informed capacity-limited intervention policies. The validation-selected logistic regression model achieved a test precision-recall area under the curve of 0.550 and a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve of 0.681. Broader student histories improved prediction of unmodified resubmission. After standardized repair and evidence gating, 519 of 544 newly generated messages contained all required components. A fixed-threshold sequential policy selected 17.8% of eligible test states and captured 25.2% of observed persistent failures. These findings support an evidence-gated progressive assistance strategy: calibrated risk guides intervention timing, recorded evidence constrains feedback content, and assistance progresses from self-checks to localized hints when warranted. The framework connects prediction, decision-making, and grounded generation while keeping their evaluation outcomes distinct.
